item.title: Daily scan · 25 Nov 2026
item.description:
Selection day: 25 Nov 2026 · America/Los_Angeles.

11 sourced selections. Source dates are original publication dates, not issue publication times.

Archived rollouts can recover a model’s reinforcement learning

A reinforcement-learning run can leave useful training data behind in the answers it generates. Starting from the same initial model, the authors recover its learning curve by fitting those saved answers in their original order, including incorrect ones and ignoring rewards. This suggests preserving rollout archives for reuse. The experiments recover existing training progress in models up to four billion parameters; they do not remove the cost of the original run.

Source: Jiayi Sheng and coauthors · 2026-11-24 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-24T18:38:06Z; no later revision listed at retrieval. The Nov25 announcement is not the submission date..

Limits: Same initialization for recovery; language models up to 4B. A last-step batch worked for Qwen3-1.7B but not SmolLM2-360M, where 50 late batches closed most of the gap.

Read scope: Submission history; HTML sections 1–4.5, conclusion and Appendix A settings, with close reading of recovery Table 2. Population analysis read, not formally proved. No training or independent replication.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-33102

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33102

Versioned methods, recovery results and limits: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.33102v1

Human disagreements help uncover an automated judge’s biases

HuB-J starts with cases where people and automated judges disagree, then uses a language model to identify possible sources of bias. It rewrites rejected answers at different strengths to measure which features change a judge’s decision. Comprehensive lists produced frequent preference changes in the tested judges. These are controlled rewriting tests, and the rewrites did not always preserve meaning, so the results need care when applied to ordinary evaluations.

Source: Hamin Koo and coauthors · 2026-11-24 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-24T18:05:47Z; no later revision listed at retrieval. NeurIPS2026 is the stated venue, not a separately verified release date..

Limits: Ten annotators each checked 25 pairs for meaning preservation: 86% overall, 70% for narratives. The 31.8% mitigation figure is regression-estimated bias attribution, not a real-world correction rate. Author-linked code returned 404.

Read scope: Submission history; HTML methods, results, limitations, dataset splits, human checks and regression appendix. Author-linked repository and project-page availability checks. No code execution or independent replication.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-33065

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33065

Versioned audit methods, results and human-check limits: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.33065v1

Agent policies can transfer without copying full reasoning

CoT-Proxy teaches an agent from a stronger model’s actions, optionally adding short reasoning summaries. The student’s reasoning block stays empty during training, and a replay penalty limits drift from its starting model. The authors report gains on application tasks and code repairs when the student later reasons for itself. The strongest code-repair setting used one training run, so its headline gain has limited evidence about repeatability.

Source: Dawid J. Kopiczko and coauthors · 2026-11-24 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-24T18:58:53Z; no later revision listed at retrieval. The Nov25 announcement is not the submission date..

Limits: Two student sizes and two environments with LoRA. AppWorld averages three seeds; closed-teacher SWE-bench uses one seed, 2,970 successful training trajectories and five passes. No paper-specific implementation was verified.

Read scope: Submission history; HTML methods, setup, main results, selected ablations, conclusion and paired comparisons. No code execution or independent replication; no paper-specific implementation link verified.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-33148

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.33148

Versioned training recipe, results and seed accounting: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.33148v1

Four-bit reward models can change which answer wins

Reducing a reward model to four-bit weights can leave its benchmark accuracy almost unchanged while altering which answers it prefers. Across the tested models, many preference decisions flipped, especially when the original scores were close. Downstream selection often chose a different response but usually kept the same final answer. The useful check is decision and answer disagreement; these experiments do not establish a uniform decline in quality.

Source: Omkar Shewale and coauthors · 2026-11-20 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-20T05:39:34Z.

Limits: Weight-only 4-bit; math-only downstream selection, two reward-model families, one generator and arbiter. Harm varies by model and quantizer. The Gaussian model fails for generative judges; margin routing does not beat plain top-k.

Read scope: Submission history; selected full-text setup, churn, harm, downstream selection, diagnostic comparisons and limitations. Full HTML captured; no execution or reproduction.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-27155

primary paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27155

versioned primary full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.27155v1

A small scorer chooses pretraining documents as learning changes

DAiSy learns which documents to train on as the language model changes. A small scoring model learns from documents already used in training, then ranks new candidates without running the full language model on each one. The authors report gains over several selection baselines in small language-model pretraining. Target choice matters: steering strongly toward benchmark-like material can worsen general web-text performance, and each training configuration was run only once.

Source: Simin Fan and Martin Jaggi · 2026-11-24 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-24T09:54:25Z; no later revision listed at retrieval. The linked repository predates the paper; its creation and push timestamps do not establish a separate public release date..

Limits: Only 124M and 720M English models; multilingual experiments use 124M. One random seed per run. Embeddings must be computed for the corpus first. Larger candidate windows can worsen general-web loss; improved target-task loss is not a universal quality gain or a zero-overhead claim. The 5.6% figure is analytic FLOP overhead. Equal-token 124M runs took 32.6–43.4 GPU-hours versus 28.8 for uniform sampling; precomputed embeddings add prior cost.

Read scope: Read submission history; full-text method, target construction, main Tables 1–2, cost accounting and limitations; official README, complete tree and online scorer/ridge/selection code. Inspected code only; no training, model downloads, API inference or independent replication.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-32294

Primary paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32294

Versioned full text, results and cost limits: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.32294v1

Author-linked reference implementation: https://github.com/Olivia-fsm/daisy_official

Generate the record first to build labeled conversation data

Conversim creates a structured record first, then asks a model to write a dialogue from it. Explicit choices about speakers and topic order make the generated examples more varied. A small German clinical extraction test improved when trained on these varied examples. This is a useful pattern for building labeled conversation data, but the evaluation used acted scripts from the same generator and does not establish reliability on real consultations.

Source: Konrad Stolte and Toni Fetzer · 2026-11-24 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-24T13:52:24Z; no later revision listed at retrieval. Repository metadata predates the paper (created September 9; pushed October 23); corpus generation dates are not public release dates..

Limits: One German STI/HIV schema and one training run per condition; the held-out conversations are generated scripts performed by people. The inspected validator checks dialogue format rather than factual completeness. Audio and the earlier control records are withheld. Synthetic profiles are designed coverage, not a population sample.

Read scope: Read submission history and full-text generation, corpus, diversity, downstream test and limits. Inspected complete repository tree, README/data manifest/schema, generation and validation code, plus one main and one held-out record/script pair. No library run, training, audio generation or score replication.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-32631

Primary paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.32631

Versioned full text and small downstream test: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.32631v1

Author-linked generator and data: https://github.com/cronn/conversim

Dataset scope, split descriptions and restrictions: https://github.com/cronn/conversim/tree/master/dataset

Calendar tests expose a gap between synthetic and realistic questions

CivilTime-Bench tests calendar calculations such as daylight saving changes and time-zone conversions. The benchmark pairs 60,011 generated training examples with synthetic tests and 500 realistic scenarios written by a model and checked by people. Fine-tuning scores are much higher on synthetic tests than realistic ones. The public artifact has gaps, so these results need care before using this benchmark to select a scheduling assistant.

Source: Melika Shirian and coauthors · 2026-11-23 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-23T03:40:13Z; no later revision listed at retrieval..

Limits: HumanTime-500 is absent from the inspected repository tree. The published scorer accepts one ambiguity alternative, conflicting with the strict full-answer paper protocol. Some prediction dumps are incomplete or invalid.

Read scope: Read submission history, HTML dataset/protocol, Table 6 and coverage appendix, repository README/tree and evaluate.py. No model runs or score replication.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#arxiv-2611-29972

primary paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29972

versioned primary full text: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.29972v1

official code and synthetic data: https://github.com/CivilTime-Bench/CivilTime-Bench

Audit benchmark tasks before trusting their scores

A benchmark can reject a correct solution when its instructions, files, and grader disagree. This paper combines the authors’ reviews of 749 tasks across eight benchmarks and reports that most confirmed defects deny credit to compliant work. Its audit categories suggest concrete checks for evaluation builders, but the study does not measure how repaired tasks would change model rankings.

Source: Authors (arXiv preprint) · 2026-11-20 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC): 2026-11-20T13:50:06Z.

Limits: Reviews come from the authors’ own lab and shared rubric; model cohorts were not rerun on repaired harnesses. Isolation and curation comparisons are observational across benchmarks with different domains and workflows. Public repository tree contains reports but no .py or .csv files, so manuscript claims about archived scripts/CSV summaries were not verified.

Read scope: Read abstract/history; HTML §2.1, §3.2, §4.1–4.2, §5–6; official repository README and recursive tree. Did not audit each underlying task or reproduce scores.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#benchmarks-last-exam

abstract and history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27622

paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.27622v1

official reports: https://github.com/ZekkiCat/Benchmarks-Last-Exam

Langfuse launches Topics in public beta

Langfuse launched Topics in public beta to group production traces by what users ask, their sentiment, outcomes and reported issues. Teams can inspect the underlying conversations and use recurring problems to design more targeted evaluations. The tool uses models chosen by the customer, so generated group names still need review. Each new facet summary counts toward Langfuse usage, and model calls cost extra.

Source: Langfuse · 2026-11-24 · Official launch visibly dated November 24, 2026 and explicitly announces public beta today in all Langfuse Cloud regions. Official v4.86.0 release published_at is 2026-11-24T18:54:46Z (not draft or prerelease); tagged source supports access changes but does not independently attest every hosted deployment..

Limits: Company-described capabilities, not independently measured clustering accuracy or defect-detection performance. Clusters and names can change; similar conversations may have different outcomes. Recorded GENERATION inputs/outputs and configured models are required. Summary models receive selected trace content; embedding/grouping models receive summaries. Langfuse counts each new facet summary as a billable unit, with model-provider charges separate. No product account accessed, key configured or model calls made.

Read scope: Full dated official launch and current documentation covering method, setup, permissions, sample limits, interpretation, costs and unstable API. Full v4.86.0 release metadata/notes plus focused PR descriptions and pinned Topics access helper/README read. No runtime deployment, user-interface test or independent performance evaluation.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#company-langfuse-topics-beta-20261124

Official November 24 Topics public-beta announcement: https://langfuse.com/topics

Official Topics documentation: setup, interpretation and costs: https://langfuse.com/docs/observability/features/topics

Official v4.86.0 tagged release: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/releases/tag/v4.86.0

Pinned release source: Topics permission check: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/blob/v4.86.0/web/src/features/topics/topicsAccess.ts

Braintrust makes Patterns generally available

Braintrust made Patterns generally available to inspect agent traces and application logs for recurring failures and unnecessary work. Each finding links to supporting traces and its frequency, helping teams decide what deserves investigation. Teams can investigate further in Loop or a coding agent and turn evidence into tests, but the findings still need review. Usage billing starts December 7.

Source: Braintrust · 2026-11-23 · Company announcement visibly dated 23 November 2026; article:published_time and JSON-LD datePublished agree. The event is general availability after a public preview, not the first preview..

Limits: Not an independent detection-accuracy benchmark. Findings and fixes need validation; external data access remains future-facing. Patterns and Loop consume resource-based credits; billing begins December 7. Enterprise continuation requires an eligible administrator to accept updated terms by end of December 6. Current docs require logged traces, compatible model access and project Update permission; BYOC also needs a supported Loop runtime.

Read scope: Full dated company announcement, including preview-to-GA wording, workflow, billing and Enterprise opt-in. Current official enablement docs read after direct HTTP capture, including requirements, scheduling and credit exhaustion. Company customer anecdotes were not audited or repeated as general measured effects. No product used.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#company-braintrust-patterns-ga-20261123

Build better agents with Patterns — dated primary GA announcement: https://www.braintrust.dev/blog/patterns

Official enablement documentation — permissions, prerequisites and billing limits: https://docs.braintrust.dev/observe/patterns/enable

Humyn Labs raises $47 million for real-world robotics training data

Humyn Labs announced $47 million in financing: $26 million of equity led by Accel and $21 million of venture debt. It says the funding will expand hardware and software that record human work and turn it into labelled robotics training data, alongside deployment infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India. Its data-quality and provenance claims remain company statements; no open dataset or robot-performance result accompanies this announcement.

Source: Humyn Labs · 2026-11-18 · Dated primary company announcement; The primary release explicitly says November 18, 2026. Funding announcement, not a dated new dataset or general-availability product release; a separate financing close date is not stated..

Limits: The $47 million total includes $21 million debt and should not be called a $47 million equity round. Revenue, geographic reach, training readiness and verified-provenance descriptions are company claims, not independently audited measurements. The announcement does not release an open dataset or show that its data causes downstream robot performance improvements.

Read scope: Humyn Labs Raises USD 47M in Series A: Full company funding announcement, including financing split, intended use and data-capture description; revenue claim not audited.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-25/#company-humyn-series-a-20261118

Humyn Labs Raises USD 47M in Series A: https://humynlabs.ai/blog/humyn-labs-raises-usd-47m-in-series-a

item.title: Daily scan · 18 Nov 2026
item.description:
Selection day: 18 Nov 2026 · America/Los_Angeles.

13 sourced selections. Source dates are original publication dates, not issue publication times.

Eyes in the Update? Learning Where Rewards Land in Multimodal Reasoning

Gaze-RL changes which generated words receive most of a training reward, using the model's own visual representations and uncertainty rather than extra step annotations. The authors report improvements on image and video reasoning across three open model versions using the same 200-update budget. It adds training computation and cannot repair a wrong reward or visual evidence the model failed to represent.

Source: Lixuan He and coauthors · 2026-11-17 · arXiv v1 submission: 17 Nov 2026 at 09:11:42 UTC.

Limits: Cannot correct erroneous verifier rewards or weak visual representations; full causal support computation adds quadratic response-length training work; Qwen NExT-QA remains below the base checkpoint; no independent replication

Read scope: Complete primary HTML captured; submission history, method, experimental setup, main tables, limitations, compute appendix and selected ablations read; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#gaze-rl

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22438

Full paper, experiments and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.22438v1

Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models

Lee audited four preference-tuned LLaVA checkpoints and found lower hallucination scores came with missed object categories and no significant object-F1 gain on CHAIR. Making the base model stop earlier reproduced 58–86% of the hallucination reduction for three checkpoints across two COCO sets. The result supports measuring coverage alongside hallucination, but covers one backbone with greedy decoding, and the stopping comparison does not establish what caused training changes.

Source: Hansang Lee · 2026-11-17 · arXiv v1 submission: 17 Nov 2026 at 18:24:58 UTC.

Limits: One LLaVA-1.5-7B backbone, greedy decoding and one detailed-caption prompt; stopping shares are reproduction ratios, not causal training effects; more than half of categories appended by the restoration method are hallucinated; no independent replication

Read scope: Complete primary HTML captured; submission history, recall matching, checkpoint validation, main results, restoration controls, discussion and limitations read; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#say-less-hallucinate-less

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23179

Full paper, matched-recall results and limits: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23179v1

Get Hint-Augmented GRPO Done Right Through Activation Steering

ASH trains a steering vector alongside reinforcement learning so a model can retain some benefit of hints when the test question has none. The authors report gains across four small language models on mathematics and reasoning benchmarks. Its generation budget matches comparison methods, but training takes about 1.5 times as long as the standard reinforcement-learning baseline, and eight-attempt scores do not measure single-answer reliability.

Source: Khiem Le, Ting Hua and Nitesh V. Chawla · 2026-11-17 · arXiv v1 submission: 17 Nov 2026 at 17:43:28 UTC.

Limits: About 1.5× GRPO training time despite a matched generation budget; four 1B–4B models; pass@8 differs from single-answer accuracy; training-seed uncertainty not reported; inference still injects one learned steering vector; no independent replication

Read scope: Complete primary HTML captured; submission history, steering method, training setup, main results, transfer tests and limitations read; code not executed and results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#activation-steering-hinting

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23124

Full paper, training budget and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23124v1

Regularized Score Centering

Asynchronous reinforcement learning trains on responses from older model versions, and that gap can destabilize updates. RSC penalizes large departures from the model that generated a training batch, while adjusting updates to account for that older model. The authors report stronger agent-task results and more sample-efficient training, but most controlled tasks use fixed refresh schedules, and fully asynchronous software experiments use one seed per configuration.

Source: Hao Bai and coauthors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 19:12:50 UTC; later index announcement dates are not the submission date.

Limits: Controlled agent tasks use fixed refresh intervals and three seeds; WebShop is essentially tied with IS-PPOClip; fully asynchronous software comparisons use single runs and adding KL hurts one lower-learning-rate TIS comparison; theoretical guarantees require stated fitting assumptions; no independent replication

Read scope: Complete primary HTML captured; submission history, methodology, failure diagnostics, controlled agent results and asynchronous software setup read; proof details not independently checked and results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#regularized-score-centering

Paper and original submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21791

Full paper, agent experiments and assumptions: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21791v1

MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables

MM-ReportBench tests whether an AI can turn tables into a report whose text and charts agree with the data. Its authors assembled 386 tasks and use separate judges for narrative and visualization quality, reporting that one combined judge inflated scores by 8–12 points. The models were accessed during November 2025–January 2026, which limits the results' relevance to current model choices.

Source: Teng Lin and Nan Tang / HKUST(GZ) · 2026-11-17 · arXiv v1 submission history: 17 November 2026, 10:06:56 UTC. The paper states its model-access window was November 2025–January 2026..

Limits: GPT-4o-based judges and an older model-access window constrain interpretation. Text-only systems receive zero visual score. Findings are author-reported; no experiments or judge outputs were reproduced.

Read scope: Read the arXiv abstract and submission history, plus HTML sections III, IV and relevant appendix descriptions covering construction, judging, experimental setup, results and error analysis; selected sections rather than a cover-to-cover read.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#mm-reportbench

arXiv abstract and dated submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22514

Original paper: methods, evaluation window and results: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.22514v1

MentalGrid tests spatial changes without intermediate visual feedback

MentalGrid asks models to track where objects and an observer move after a sequence of instructions, without showing the intervening images. The authors supply 3,356 questions and train a 3B model with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning. They report a large gain over its base model, but the benchmark uses simulated scenes and leaves out collisions and material properties.

Source: Jiachun Li, Zhuoran Jin, Kang Liu and Jun Zhao / Chinese Academy of Sciences · 2026-11-17 · arXiv v1 submission history: 17 November 2026, 10:31:56 UTC; the record identifies Findings of EMNLP 2026..

Limits: All scenes are simulated; object pose, materials and collisions are excluded. Human results and some expensive-model results use the tiny subset, so those scores are not full-set comparisons. Results were not replicated.

Read scope: Read arXiv abstract/history and original HTML sections 1–4 and Limitations, including the dataset pipeline, evaluation setup, Tables 1–3 and training description; selected sections rather than a complete paper read.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#mentalgrid-spatialwalker

arXiv abstract and dated submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22541

Original paper: MentalGrid construction, results and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.22541v1

DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images

DominoBench uses pairs of almost identical pictures to test whether a model can predict a simulated chain reaction. One small physical change flips the answer, exposing models that describe a plausible sequence without calculating the outcome. The author releases 854 items and reports weak unaided performance; supplying the deciding calculation helps, but also supplies information that a still image cannot reveal.

Source: Emilio Ferrara · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submitted 16 November 2026, 01:24:42 UTC; v2 revised 17 November 2026, 07:40:39 UTC. The item date is the original submission, not the revision or later discovery date..

Limits: The scenes use one 2D line-art style, human accuracy was not measured, and coverage differs by model. The strongest hint supplies hidden quantities, so its improvement does not establish unaided physical inference. Results were not replicated.

Read scope: Read the arXiv abstract/history, original HTML construction, protocol, metrics, results and limitations sections, and the official Hugging Face dataset card; selected sections rather than a complete paper read.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#dominobench

arXiv original and revised submission dates: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20385

Original paper: experimental protocol and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20385v2

Official dataset card and evaluation harness: https://huggingface.co/datasets/emilioferrara/DominoBench

CAE-Bench tests whether agent-built engineering solvers generalize

CAE-Bench tests an agent's engineering solver on physical inputs it did not see while writing the code. The authors evaluate 12 models on 80 computational tasks and report cases where solvers pass the public examples but fail held-out inputs. This is useful for checking reusable simulation software, although complete grading needs maintainer-held files and the authors flag uncertainty in some reference data.

Source: Zhiyu Zhou, Tianyou Liu and collaborators · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission history: 16 November 2026, 15:40:43 UTC. The RC7 public paper-snapshot release separately shows 14 November; its tag's 20261029 component is not the publication date..

Limits: Full grading requires maintainer-held inputs, references and grading configurations. Appendix B says not all reference data are guaranteed credible enough. Fixed-problem and varying-input scores answer different questions. No solvers or reference data were independently tested.

Read scope: Read the arXiv abstract/history, original HTML task/protocol and release/reconstruction appendix sections, official repository README and public RC7 release notes; selected sections rather than a complete paper read.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#cae-bench

arXiv abstract and dated submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21273

Original paper: tasks, references and reconstruction limits: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21273v1

Official benchmark repository and scoring scope: https://github.com/AXeonV/CAE-Bench

MLPerf Training v6.1 adds agentic RL and generative recommendation workloads

MLCommons released MLPerf Training v6.1 results, adding an agentic reinforcement-learning workload and a generative recommendation workload. The round includes 250 submissions from 25 submitters and provides measured training-system comparisons under benchmark rules. The results help infrastructure teams compare submitted configurations, while the article's broader speedup ratios remain derived analysis and do not describe every training job.

Source: MLCommons · 2026-11-16 · MLCommons' analysis is visibly dated 17 November 2026 and explicitly states that verified v6.1 Closed-division results were published 16 November at 08:00 Pacific. The item uses that result-release date..

Limits: The four unchanged benchmarks support specific cross-round comparisons; new benchmarks do not have prior-round baselines. Ratios in the analysis are MLCommons-derived rather than official standalone scores. No submitted systems or raw result logs were reproduced.

Read scope: Read the official MLCommons analysis, benchmark-update sections, comparison definitions, cited result descriptions and limitations. The external spreadsheet, result explorer and supplemental PDF were not inspected.

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#mlperf-training-v61

MLCommons release analysis with result-publication date and benchmark changes: https://mlcommons.org/2026/11/mlperf-training-v6-1-insights/

Guidepoint launches an expert-data business for AI training and evaluation

Guidepoint publicly launched Guidepoint Labs after more than six months of work in stealth. The business supplies expert-written training examples, preference data and evaluations, including tasks and grading rubrics for reinforcement-learning environments. It says it already serves frontier labs and enterprises, but its launch announcement does not provide a controlled test showing that these services improve model performance.

Source: Guidepoint · 2026-11-18 · Visible official press-release dateline: November 18, 2026.

Limits: Company announcement and self-reported adoption; no independent service-quality evaluation reviewed; the cited clinical-trial benchmark is a separate earlier research result

Read scope: Full official press release, including visible dateline and service list; no customer contracts, delivered datasets or underlying clinical-trial benchmark inspected

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#guidepoint-labs-launch

Guidepoint Labs launch and service scope: https://www.guidepoint.com/pressreleases/guidepoint-unveils-guidepoint-labs-to-power-the-next-frontier-of-ai-training-and-evaluation/

LanceDB raises $57.5 million for multimodal training-data infrastructure

LanceDB announced a $57.5 million Series B to expand its platform for preparing and using multimodal training data. The company describes a shared system where researchers can curate examples and run training workflows without moving between separate stores. The funding is an announced completed raise; broader data-preparation and loading improvements remain development plans, and the post's performance figures are company claims.

Source: LanceDB · 2026-11-17 · Visible date beneath the headline of the official company announcement.

Limits: Performance, customer and growth figures are self-reported; planned investments in preparation, loading and caching are not completed releases

Read scope: Full official funding announcement and product-direction sections, including the visible publication date and attributed customer statements; no product execution or performance replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#lancedb-series-b

LanceDB funding announcement and development plans: https://www.lancedb.com/blog/lancedb-series-b-funding

Scale examines diversity in 20,000 hours of robot training data

Scale analyzed a 20,000-hour slice of robot teleoperation data to measure variety beyond recording hours. Its analysis finds that the tested vision-only representations group clips more strongly by room type than by action, while object labels have a long tail. These checks describe the company's data and model representations; they do not establish which diversity choices improve a robot's success on new tasks.

Source: Scale Labs · 2026-11-17 · Visible official article date: 11/17/2026.

Limits: One 20,000-hour corpus slice and selected encoders; the strongest verb representation also receives the verb in its text input; downstream policy gains remain an open question

Read scope: Full official article, methods appendix, nearest-neighbor analysis and stated input-confounding caveat; underlying corpus and model code not inspected; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#scale-robot-data-diversity

Scale's robot-data analysis and methods appendix: https://labs.scale.com/blog/measuring-robot-data-diversity

Scale launches hospital agents tied to workflow-specific evaluations

Scale launched five hospital-operations applications for work such as scheduling referrals and reviewing patient records. The company says the agents run inside each health system's environment and are checked against evaluations built around its workflows. This is a product-availability announcement, not evidence of clinical benefit: the post gives no controlled results for the new applications, and its cited burnout study concerns a separate documentation tool.

Source: Scale AI · 2026-11-16 · Visible official article byline: November 16, 2026.

Limits: Availability and deployment properties are company claims; no controlled outcomes for the new applications; the cited 2025 burnout study does not evaluate this release

Read scope: Full official launch post, five application descriptions, evaluation section and availability statement; cited study and benchmark papers not reviewed for this item; products not executed

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-18/#scale-hospital-operations

Scale Hospital Operations release and evaluation approach: https://scale.com/blog/scaleforhospitaloperations

item.title: Daily scan · 17 Nov 2026
item.description:
Selection day: 17 Nov 2026 · America/Los_Angeles.

16 sourced selections. Source dates are original publication dates, not issue publication times.

OpenAI signs four assessors for internal alignment and safety reviews

OpenAI signed agreements with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire to assess alignment and safeguards using internal systems and evidence. The work includes examining a frontier reinforcement-learning run and checking the quality and coverage of post-training evaluations. This gives evaluators access beyond public model tests, but the announcement reports plans rather than completed findings, and publication remains subject to confidentiality redactions and possible disclosure delays.

Source: OpenAI / Goodfire / Transluce · 2026-11-16 · Original publication date; corroborated by Goodfire and Transluce announcements.

Limits: Planned assessments, not completed safety findings; negotiated access and publication restrictions; Apollo and Goodfire receive non-outcome-contingent compensation

Read scope: Official OpenAI announcement, protocol and compensation footnotes; downloaded Goodfire announcement and full Transluce pilot terms; no assessment findings or underlying models inspected

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#openai-embedded-assessments

OpenAI announcement and terms: https://openai.com/index/our-first-phase-of-embedded-assessments/

Goodfire announcement: https://www.goodfire.com/blog/announcing-our-collaboration-with-openai

Transluce pilot access and publication limits: https://transluce.org/embedded-assessment-pilot-with-openai

Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training

This study asks whether a fixed annotation budget is better spent on human or AI-generated preferences. It trains three small language-model families on helpfulness and summarization, matching estimated data costs instead of example counts. Synthetic data performs better at shared budgets and peaks early; human data catches up only in some higher-budget tests. The comparison uses estimated labor and serving prices and AI judges, so its dollar thresholds are specific to this setup.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-12 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Estimated annotation labor and proxy serving prices; 7–8B models with LoRA; AI-judged helpfulness and summarization

Read scope: Submission history; data, cost and evaluation methods; main results; limitations and selected appendices; official code README inspected; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#human-or-synthetic

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16895

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.16895v1

Official code: https://github.com/shourikb/human-or-synthetic

Synthetic preference data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/liteshadow4/synthetic-pref-tulu3

Benchleaking: Benchmark recall in base models

Qin and colleagues tested whether base language models could reproduce benchmark questions and answers absent from their prompts. They found large differences across four models and recalculated scores with recalled examples marked wrong. This gives evaluation teams a way to check whether high scores depend on recall, although some closely related question pairs can be reconstructed without previous exposure.

Source: Yiwei Qin and coauthors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 16:10:16 UTC.

Limits: Observed matches need benchmark-specific interpretation: WinoGrande twin questions can be reconstructed without exposure. The adjusted score is a conservative scoring rule, not a causal estimate of a model's ability without contamination. Author-linked code returned 404 when checked.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, continuation-audit method, score construction and matching-rules appendix in HTML; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#benchleaking

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21315

Full paper, including matching rules: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21315v1

Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle

A model can earn a higher training reward while giving worse reasons for a decision. This study creates access-control tasks whose correct reasons can be computed exactly, then trains models with deliberately imperfect checkers while measuring the true score. Some checkers reward padding explanations with irrelevant details; others stop providing useful feedback or mainly add noise. The patterns recur across the authors' training configurations, but the size of the damage does not, and the tasks use bounded policy abstractions.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Bounded authorization-policy testbed and abstracted public policies; damage magnitude did not replicate across the authors' configurations; artifact release not verified

Read scope: Submission history; oracle and verifier construction; main results, replication findings, limitations and selected appendices; code availability statement inspected; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#optimistic-verifiers

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21538

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21538v1

Toloka Arena adds ten-category failure profiles for enterprise agents

Toloka added failure profiles to its Arena, showing ten kinds of mistakes rather than only an overall score. It reports that about half of failed attempts among the ten leading models passed a conversation assessment even though system records were wrong. The profiles can help teams choose what to test or retrain, but these are results from Toloka's simulated workflows.

Source: Toloka · 2026-11-16 · Original publication date (article and dated HTML metadata).

Limits: Company-run simulated enterprise workflows; error categories can overlap; reported rates are shares of all attempts rather than mutually exclusive shares of failures

Read scope: Full official product/research post and stated scoring definitions; raw trajectories and grading code not inspected; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#toloka-arena-failure-profiles

Toloka failure-profile release and scoring definitions: https://toloka.ai/blog/what-the-scores-dont-tell-you-about-ai-agents-on-toloka-arena/

Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning

When a cheap safety checker sends only uncertain answers to a stronger judge, confidently missed harm escapes review. This paper tests how that weakness changes during training and after the checker is updated. Confidently missed harmful answers often become a larger share of remaining harm even when their total amount falls. The proposed checks distinguish these trends, but evidence covers two small models and two reward judges, and human review sometimes disagrees with automated measures.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Two 7–8B policies, one commercial judge and one open guard, mainly two seeds; limited human audit; helpfulness trade-offs vary by model

Read scope: Submission history; validation protocol; reward conditions, experimental setup, results, limitations and human-audit appendix; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#jev-as-a-reward

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20955

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20955v1

Prolific adds a visual editor for multimodal data collection and evaluation

Prolific has renamed AI Task Builder to Task Builder and added a drag-and-drop editor with the same capabilities as its API. Teams can collect or compare text, images, audio and video, including feedback tied to individual video frames. This consolidates evaluation setup, but the announcement does not provide a controlled comparison of data quality or turnaround time.

Source: Prolific · 2026-11-16 · Original publication date; corroborated by the product-update index.

Limits: An expansion of an existing product, not a newly created participant network; no controlled quality or speed comparison

Read scope: Full dated official release, feature descriptions and availability statement; product not executed and participant quality not independently tested

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#prolific-task-builder

Prolific Task Builder release: https://www.prolific.com/resources/evaluate-and-collect-text-images-audio-and-video-with-task-builder

Official product-update index: https://www.prolific.com/resources?type=product-updates

GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model

This model judges a reasoning step using earlier steps and their assessments plus the rest of the proposed solution. It learns to check consistency, the step itself and whether the solution stays on task. The authors report better error detection and guided mathematics search, but checking unfinished candidates requires generating their remaining steps, increasing cost. Tests of whether this improves complete interactive agent tasks remain future work.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Online search must complete candidate trajectories; cost ablation reports +71.7% tokens and +42.4% latency; interactive agent success not tested

Read scope: Submission history; model and dataset construction; main benchmark results, test-time search, inference-cost analysis and selected appendices; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#gprm

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20755

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20755v1

Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization

Liu and colleagues built 32 tasks that ask coding agents to speed up working scientific programs while keeping their outputs correct. Agents can test changes during development, but a separate checker measures the final program. The reported results show that build settings and interacting code changes can matter greatly; the scores describe complete agent setups on fixed CPU workloads, so they do not isolate model ability.

Source: Bowen Liu and coauthors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 10:52:59 UTC.

Limits: Scores mix model, harness and compute choices; the main table uses one run per agent, with repeats for two. Speedups are relative to differently tuned task baselines at fixed CPU workloads; trajectory analyses use older v1.0 runs.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, benchmark construction, scoring protocol, main results and limitations in HTML; official project page; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#accelerate-bench

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20882

Full paper, benchmark protocol and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20882v1

Official project, reported results and access requirements: https://acceleratebench.com/

Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data

Kua and Song tested whether generated images help when the image generator learns only from the same training set as the classifier. Across six datasets, benefits were generally smaller when generated images differed more from real ones or the starting classifier was already strong. Ordinary image transformations matched most of the largest gains under equal training steps, so generating more images was not automatically worthwhile.

Source: Daniel Kua and Yan Song · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 17:47:45 UTC.

Limits: The estimated mismatch is a lower bound, and the theoretical bound explains trends without predicting gain magnitude or direction; stability and dependence terms remain unquantified. Results do not test externally pretrained generators.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, experimental setup, theoretical-bound interpretation, equal-step augmentation comparison and conclusion in HTML; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#generative-augmentation-no-external-data

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21467

Full paper and experiment protocol: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21467v1

Policy Optimization With Multiple Verifiers via Pareto Rankings

When several checks score an answer, counting passed checks can hide which requirements improved. POLPO trains on comparisons where one answer passes every check another answer passes, plus at least one more; it leaves conflicting cases unordered. The authors report gains in coding and following multiple instructions. The method receives no learning signal when none of the sampled answers clearly improves on another, and some coding tests use only one training seed.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-14 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: No dominance means no comparison signal; APPS and AceCode use one training seed; benefits depend on automatic checks and small-model benchmark settings

Read scope: Submission history; partial-order objective; coding and instruction-following result tables; conclusion, reproducibility statement and selected computation/evaluation appendices; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#polpo

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19064

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.19064v1

SAJ-MTL: Modeling demographic differences in annotation

Gupta and colleagues built a model that keeps track of which demographic groups label a post and which groups the post targets. This preserves differences in how people judge harmful text and lets users choose how to weight those views. The authors report better predictions on two datasets, but groups with sparse data were excluded and the method does not guarantee fair moderation.

Source: Soumyajit Gupta, Maria De-Arteaga and Matthew Lease · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 17:42:54 UTC.

Limits: Experiments cover two toxicity datasets and four race groups; three Measuring Hate Speech groups were omitted because annotator-target pairs were sparse. Group attributes remain sensitive, and improved prediction does not guarantee fairness.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, methods overview, dataset and label protocol, results tables, discussion and ethical considerations in HTML; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#saj-mtl

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21458

Full paper and results tables: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21458v1

micro1 describes fixing infrastructure errors that distorted agent evaluations

micro1 describes changes to the system that runs and grades its AI-agent evaluations. It now separates infrastructure failures from wrong answers, retries failed attempts and checks each model's actual output limits before a benchmark run. The company reports that correcting one token-limit problem raised a model's score from 0.33 to 0.48, but this is an internal case study rather than independently reproduced evidence.

Source: micro1 · 2026-11-10 · Original publication date; retrospective about earlier infrastructure changes.

Limits: Engineering retrospective, not a new product launch; anonymous model and benchmark in cited score example; internal measurements not independently reproduced

Read scope: Full official engineering report, especially failure handling, frozen task versions and release-day harness limits; infrastructure and score corrections not executed or independently audited

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#micro1-rollout-reliability

micro1 engineering report: https://www.micro1.ai/blog/the-only-bottleneck-should-be-the-model

Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment

Preference training usually stores intermediate model activity for backpropagation, which consumes GPU memory. This method uses differences between preferred and rejected answers to choose a small set of directions for trying weight changes without backpropagation. The authors report similar judged answer preferences to standard training while using about 59% less peak memory at 2,048 tokens. It needs three forward passes per update, so lower memory does not establish faster training; evidence covers one small model and dataset.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: One Qwen2.5-1.5B model and HH-RLHF dataset; LLM judges; three forward passes per update; no demonstrated speed advantage

Read scope: Submission history; optimization method; experimental setup; complete pairwise and memory results; limitations and hyperparameter/evaluation appendices; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#ca-zodpo

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20635

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20635v1

Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows

Bathla built six simulated environments for Indian travel, payments, tax, forms and customer support. Their 321 public tasks are checked by written rules that recompute results from made-up records. This lets teams inspect why an agent passed without relying on another AI judge. The reported tests use one run per task, and the simplified rules and partly machine-produced language examples limit what the scores show about real services.

Source: Daksh Bathla / Navital Labs · 2026-11-16 · arXiv v1 submission: 16 Nov 2026 at 11:35:01 UTC; new paper about software first released 27 Oct 2026.

Limits: Trip scores include one format-repair retry; some results use earlier grader versions. The rules simplify practice, and the Tamil, Bengali and Marathi examples were not reviewed by native speakers. Private held-out tasks are not inspectable.

Read scope: Submission history; abstract, environment definitions, grader protocol, reported results and limitations in HTML; official repository README and GitHub release metadata; no code execution or independent replication

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#navital-gym

Paper and submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20924

Full paper, grader details and limitations: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.20924v1

Official code, tasks and license: https://github.com/Navitallabs/navital-gym

Initial software release, dated 27 Oct 2026: https://github.com/Navitallabs/navital-gym/releases/tag/v1.0.0

Surge compares coding agents on engineering judgment

Surge tested five coding agents on its sudo L7 benchmark, which evaluates engineering judgment as well as working code. It reports that all three Claude models outscored the two GPT models, with similar functional correctness but larger differences in communication and spotting hidden risks. These company-run results have not been independently reproduced and do not establish how the agents will perform on other workloads.

Source: Surge AI · 2026-11-13 · Original publication date (article and publication metadata).

Limits: Company-run comparison; exact task count and agent software assignment are not reported in the reviewed article body; results not independently reproduced

Read scope: Official article body, examples and current web extraction; chart scores not transcribed; exact task count and model-to-harness assignment not verified; tasks, rubrics and runs not independently audited or reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-17/#surge-sudo-l7-model-comparison

Surge comparison and evaluation setup: https://surgehq.ai/blog/claude-vs-gpt-software-engineering

item.title: Daily scan · 16 Nov 2026
item.description:
Selection day: 16 Nov 2026 · America/Los_Angeles.

18 sourced selections. Source dates are original publication dates, not issue publication times.

PORT: Preference Optimization via Robust Token-Level Reweighting

A preferred answer can contain mistakes, and a rejected answer can still contain useful text. PORT compares how likely the model considers small pieces of each answer and uses their ranks within a training batch to change how strongly those pieces affect learning. The aim is to learn from imperfect preference labels without letting unreliable pieces dominate; the method was less reliable with very small batches.

Source: PORT authors · 2026-11-09 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Small-batch sensitivity; sufficient theory assumptions; multi-turn extension untested

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#port

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12763

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.12763v1

Code: https://github.com/osu-srml/PORT

VEPO: Mitigating Multilingual Hallucinations in LVLMs via Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization

Image-answering models can mention objects that are absent, especially when answering in languages with less training data. VEPO uses English questions to locate key image regions, then trains with the same answer paired with either the full image or an image with those regions hidden. This encourages answers backed by visible evidence in other languages. The reported tests cover Chinese, French and Hindi; Hindi training also needed English examples.

Source: VEPO authors · 2026-11-13 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: English-centric transfer; Hindi required English-pair mixing

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#vepo

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18096

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18096v1

PrivacyPR: Real-world privacy fixes for code-review evaluation

PrivacyPR tests whether AI code reviewers can spot problems that expose or misuse personal information. It turns real privacy fixes accepted by developers into review tasks by putting the faulty code back. Asking agents to focus on privacy helped them find more problems, but they still raised false alarms and some dataset labels were uncertain.

Source: PrivacyPR authors · 2026-11-13 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Small evaluation subset; both annotators endorsed 72% of automated GDPR-principle labels

Read scope: Abstract and submission history; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#privacypr

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18293

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.18293v1

Mercor announces $750 million Series D at a $20 billion valuation

Mercor announced a $750 million funding deal at a $20 billion valuation. It says the financing will support tools that use human expertise to train AI agents and test them on realistic workplace tasks. The deal includes employee share sales, and Mercor did not say how much is new money for the business.

Source: Mercor · 2026-11-10 · Original publication date.

Limits: Primary-versus-secondary capital split undisclosed; funding and valuation are not revenue

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#mercor-series-d

Mercor announcement: https://www.mercor.com/blog/series-d/

Reuters reporting: https://www.aol.com/articles/ai-training-startup-mercor-valued-153730000.html

FlinkEval: Synthetic data for streaming-SQL evaluation

FlinkEval tests whether AI can write database queries for data that keeps arriving, such as a stream of transactions. It creates requests and matching queries, then checks them on a working streaming database. This reveals problems with timing and unclear requests, but some reported scores judge query quality even when the queries could not run.

Source: FlinkEval authors · 2026-11-12 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Single deployment; five-model study excluded 115 windowing cases affected by an engine defect; 81 background DML cases not executable, scored by judged SQL quality

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#flinkeval

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17093

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.17093v1

Scale and Singapore's IMDA introduce SG-LegalClarify

SG-LegalClarify tests whether AI asks for missing facts before answering questions about Singapore law. Models can ask a simulated user for details, and AI judges check their answers against criteria written by legal experts. The results reveal gaps in gathering facts and applying the law, but the score counts individual criteria rather than fully correct answers.

Source: Scale / IMDA · 2026-11-12 · Original publication date.

Limits: Reported criterion-satisfaction scores are not overall legal accuracy; jurisdiction-specific and partly AI-judged

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#sg-legalclarify

Scale research report: https://scale.com/blog/scale-imda-legal-reasoning-benchmark

Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling

This paper asks whether clues about how people read can help a model judge which answer people would prefer. It predicts how long a reader might look at each word, spreads that signal to nearby words, and adds it to an answer-scoring model. The reported gains concern preference prediction in English; the study uses predicted gaze, not new eye-tracking measurements, and does not test whether it improves a chatbot's answers.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-10 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: English-only experiments; synthetic gaze; no downstream policy-alignment test

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#gaze-reward-modeling

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13477

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.13477v1

Nemotron-PII-Japan: Annotated synthetic Japanese business documents

NVIDIA created made-up Japanese business documents to help train and test systems that find or hide personal information. The process chooses fictional identifying details, builds documents around them and labels where those details appear. This provides examples without collecting customer documents, but the labels do not cover every relevant detail and can contain mistakes.

Source: NVIDIA · 2026-11-09 · Announcement 9 Nov; dataset card release date 10 Nov 2026.

Limits: Annotations are not exhaustive; no fixed public train/test split

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#nemotron-pii-japan

Official release article: https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-pii-japan

Dataset & license: https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-PII-Japan

Labelbox and Wipro partner on RL environments and managed enterprise agents

Labelbox and Wipro announced a partnership to help businesses train, test and use AI agents on workplace tasks. They say Wipro will help customers connect their systems and define what good work looks like, while Labelbox supplies simulated practice environments and agents that carry out tasks. The companies have not published customer results showing measurable gains from the partnership.

Source: Labelbox / Wipro · 2026-11-10 · Original publication date.

Limits: No named customer outcomes, deployment counts or measured production gains disclosed

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#labelbox-wipro

Original press release: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/labelbox-partners-with-wipro-to-scale-adoption-of-ai-agents-that-learn-from-enterprise-experience-302934232.html

Labelbox details: https://labelbox.com/blog/labelbox-wipro-partnership/

MotionGraphicsBench: Programmatic checks for generated animations

MotionGraphicsBench tests whether AI can animate supplied artwork according to a designer's instructions. Instead of comparing the result with one reference animation, readable checking programs test requested movements, timing and other properties. This allows different valid solutions and makes failures easier to inspect, but the checks measure following instructions rather than how beautiful an animation looks.

Source: Figma research · 2026-11-07 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC); release article 10 Nov 2026.

Limits: Narrow SVG motion-editing task; pass/fail measures instruction compliance rather than aesthetic quality

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#motiongraphicsbench

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10592

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10592v1

Official release article: https://huggingface.co/blog/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench

AERO: Adaptive Ensemble-Disagreement Routing for Oracle Feedback in Sample-Efficient Online RLHF

Asking for a preference judgment on every training example can be expensive. AERO lets several answer-scoring models vote: when they disagree strongly, it requests an outside judgment; when they agree, it supplies a predicted preference itself. This focuses the feedback budget on examples where the models are uncertain. The experiments used a fixed AI scoring model as the outside judge, so the reported savings still need testing with human feedback.

Source: AERO authors · 2026-11-07 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Deterministic reward-model oracle; no real human-feedback evaluation

Read scope: Submission history, methods and limitations; code not executed; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#aero

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10750

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10750v1

Code: https://github.com/Shrey-Singhal/AERO

Shaping Useful Noise: An energy-distribution audit for synthetic images

This paper asks how to choose useful synthetic images for training visual models. It compares the distributions of confidence scores that the same image model assigns to real and synthetic images. The comparison helped predict training results, but its proposed image selection method was checked using an existing model's features and still needs testing through new model training.

Source: Paper authors · 2026-11-09 · arXiv v1 submission (UTC).

Limits: Curation intervention reports frozen-feature proxies; matched pretraining remains future work

Read scope: Primary paper / release and stated limitations; results not reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#shaping-useful-noise

Paper & submission history: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11962

Full paper: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.11962v1

Turing describes turning connected company archives into RL benchmarks

Turing describes turning connected company records into simulated workplaces where AI agents can practice real tasks. It says automated checks score the work, letting AI labs train and test agents using the context found across a company's files, messages and code. The post explains the program without giving a launch date, test results or an independent privacy audit.

Source: Turing · 2026-11-11 · Program explanation published 11 Nov; launch date unspecified.

Limits: Program explanation; no new customer, dataset size, benchmark score or privacy audit disclosed

Read scope: Dated company announcement; reported outcomes not independently reproduced

Inspect this selection: https://sciencetostartup.com/daily/2026-11-16/#turing-company-archives

Turing program details: https://www.turing.com/blog/company-data-ai-benchmarks

OmniSynth: Stress-testing synthetic-health-data quality metrics

OmniSynth checks how well synthetic health records preserve real data patterns, including which values are missing. It deliberately adds flaws to data to see whether measures of similarity, privacy and usefulness notice the changes. This helps expose misleading quality scores, but some measures were unstable, fairness checks are absent and testing of usefulness for later prediction tasks remains incomplete.

Surge reports targeted RL gains for NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL

The results do not describe one model with every improvement, and comparisons with other models used published scores from potentially different test setups.

Think Less, Locally: Local Preference Learning for Reasoning Compression

Reasoning models sometimes keep working after they have enough information to finish. LoCo finds these points and trains the model to prefer a shorter, checked continuation over its original longer continuation, with both starting from the same reasoning so far. This teaches where to conclude, potentially cutting the cost of generating answers. The reported tests preserve or improve accuracy on mathematics and code; benefits on tasks without checkable answers remain unproven.

See Every Block Once: Variance-Reduced Post-Training for Masked Diffusion Language Models

Masked diffusion language models build text by repeatedly filling in missing pieces. Their training estimates a learning signal from text blocks, but random selection can repeat some blocks and miss others. This paper evaluates every block once and averages the results, reducing that source of noise and improving the reported tests on one model. Its proposed use with PPO or DPO, methods used to learn from preference feedback, remains untested.
